interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each reading's stick to the line shrinking and the above-and-below count evening up, while m and c fill in with units, when you drag the line's two handles.
interactive.title: Lay the line
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A short lesson in twelve small screens. Each graph has units on both axes. Example readings sit as dots, and one straight line lies across them with a round handle at each end; drag a handle to move that end of the line. A thin stick runs straight up or down from each reading to the line, and its length is how far that reading sits from the line, in the units up the side. Above the graph a running count says how many readings sit above the line and how many below. Under the graph the law fills in: m, the gradient, worked out from two points on the line as rise ÷ run, and c, the line's value where x is 0, each with its unit. A switch marked 'through zero' pins the line at (0, 0), so it can only swing about that point.

Screens 1 to 8 use eight example readings of a motor winding: resistance R in ohms (Ω) up the side, temperature T in °C along, one reading every 10 °C from 10 to 80 °C. Screen 1 shows the line R = 0.04T + 10 through their middle. It touches none of them, four sit above and four below, and no stick is longer than 0.2 Ω. Screen 2 asks you to lay it yourself, starting from the line R = 0.04T + 11, which sits above every reading. Screen 3 marks two points on the line far apart, at 20 °C and 70 °C, with the step triangle between them: a rise of 2.0 Ω over a run of 50 °C gives 0.04 Ω per °C, and c = 10.8 − 0.04 × 20 = 10.0 Ω, the line carried back to 0 °C (dashed below the readings). Screen 5 turns the pin on. The line swings to R = 0.26T, and the count still reads four and four, but the sticks grow to 7.9 Ω at 10 °C and 7.5 Ω at 80 °C, with every reading above on the left and every one below on the right: the line is tilted. Screen 7 shows why the two points go far apart. Each height read off the line is taken as good to 0.1 Ω, drawn as a short bar at each point. Between 40 and 50 °C the rise of 0.4 Ω could be anything from 0.2 to 0.6 Ω, a gradient from 0.02 to 0.06 Ω per °C; between 20 and 70 °C the rise of 2.0 Ω could be 1.8 to 2.2 Ω, a gradient from 0.036 to 0.044. The same slip of the eye is a small part of a big rise. Screen 9 shows a spring: force F in newtons (N) up the side, its extension x in millimetres along. Six readings from 2 to 12 mm scatter round F = 2.5x, pinned through (0, 0) because with no force there is no stretch, three above and three below. Two more, at 14 and 16 mm, fall away below the line past a mark labelled 'limit of proportionality', and the line is fitted to the straight part only. Screens 11 and 12 show six example readings of a lifting machine: the effort P in newtons needed against the load W in newtons it lifts, from 40 to 240 N.

Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Screen 2 is done with the handles, and Check passes when the count is four and four and no stick is longer than 0.4 Ω. The other puzzles show a graph and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? fills in the working. Screen 4 asks for the gradient: 0.04 Ω per °C from the line, 0.08 from the readings at 20 and 30 °C, or 25 °C per Ω, upside down. Screen 6 asks what the winding reads at 0 °C: 10.0 Ω from the law, 0 Ω from pinning the line, or 10.5 Ω, the first reading. Screen 8 asks which two points give the most trustworthy gradient: the line at 40 and 50 °C, the line at 20 and 70 °C, or the readings at 20 and 30 °C. Screen 10 asks for the spring constant: 2.5 N per mm from the straight part, 0.9 from the last two readings, or about 2.2 from 35.0 N ÷ 16 mm through zero. Screen 11 lays three lines on the machine's readings and asks which fits: P = 0.15W + 4, with six above and none below; P = 0.25W − 8, three and three but tilted, with the three above on the left; or P = 0.15W + 6, three and three spread along it. Screen 12 asks for that line's law: P = 0.15W + 6, P = 0.17W from one reading divided by its load, or P = 0.15W + 12.4 with the first reading taken as the intercept. After screen 12's Check a closing line says that laws that curve can be turned into straight lines in Exponentials and logarithms.
interactive.ignores: The readings are example values made up for the lesson, and so is how far each one strays; real readings have their own scatter. The line is laid by eye, so two careful people lay slightly different lines and get slightly different laws; the calculated line, found by a method called least squares, is not shown. Each stick is measured straight up or down, in the units up the side, because the law gives y from x. The pinned line's 0.26 is the picture's choice, one of the swings that splits the readings four and four; every swing through (0, 0) leaves long sticks at one end or both. The 0.1 Ω for reading a height off the line is a figure chosen for the picture, not a rule. The 10.0 Ω at 0 °C is the line carried back below the readings, trusting it to stay straight there. The spring's limit of proportionality sits between 12 and 14 mm only in these example readings; a real spring has its own.

explain.text:
Real readings scatter a little, so they seldom sit exactly on one line. You met the answer in The coordinate plane: one best-fit line through their middle, not dot to dot. This lesson turns that line into a law. Lay it so about as many readings sit above it as below, even if it passes through none of them,[^1] then take m and c from the line itself, not from the readings.

How strongly many materials resist current changes with temperature in approximately a straight line.[^9] Take eight example readings of a winding, one every 10 °C from 10 °C to 80 °C, rising from 10.5 Ω to 13.3 Ω. Each one strays a little from the trend, some up and some down, so a line through their middle follows the trend and not any one reading's stray. Draw a thin stick straight up or down from each reading to the line. The line R = 0.04T + 10 leaves four above and four below, and no stick is longer than 0.2 Ω. Take its gradient from two points on the line far apart: 10.8 Ω at 20 °C and 12.8 Ω at 70 °C give 2.0 Ω ÷ 50 °C = 0.04 Ω per °C. Far apart matters because you can read a height off a line only so closely. Say you read each one to within 0.1 Ω. Then a rise of 2.0 Ω could come out anywhere from 1.8 to 2.2 Ω, a gradient of 0.036 to 0.044, while between 40 and 50 °C the rise of 0.4 Ω could come out from 0.2 to 0.6 Ω, a gradient anywhere from 0.02 to 0.06. Two readings are worse still, because each brings its own stray: 10.6 Ω at 20 °C and 11.4 Ω at 30 °C give 0.8 Ω ÷ 10 °C = 0.08 Ω per °C, twice the line's. Then c comes from one point on the line, as in lesson 4: 10.8 − 0.04 × 20 = 10.0 Ω. So the law is R = 0.04T + 10, with 10.0 Ω the line carried back to 0 °C below the readings. The first reading, 10.5 Ω, is not c, because it was taken at 10 °C and has its own stray.

Counting is a check, not the whole rule. Pin the line through (0, 0) and it can only swing about that point. Swung to R = 0.26T it still leaves four readings above and four below, yet the sticks grow to 7.9 Ω at 10 °C and 7.5 Ω at 80 °C, and all four above sit on the left while all four below sit on the right. A pattern like that means the line is tilted, and here the pin is to blame: the winding still has resistance at 0 °C, so its line has no reason to pass through zero. Pin a line through zero only when the physics says y is 0 when x is 0. A spring is such a case, since with no force there is no stretch. Up to its [[limit of proportionality]], a graph of force against extension is a straight line through the origin.[^2] Example readings of a spring, from 5.2 N at 2 mm to 29.9 N at 12 mm, scatter round F = 2.5x, three above and three below, and its gradient, 30 N ÷ 12 mm = 2.5 N per mm, is the spring constant.[^10] Past 12 mm these example readings bend away below the line, to 33.2 N at 14 mm and 35.0 N at 16 mm, so fit the straight part only. Those last two alone give 1.8 N ÷ 2 mm = 0.9 N per mm, which is not the spring constant.

That is how the course's puzzle is answered: plot the winding's readings, lay one line through their middle, and read its two numbers as ohms per degree and ohms at 0 °C. The readings here are made-up examples and the line is laid by eye, a simplified picture: two careful people lay slightly different lines, and textbooks add that a method called least squares calculates the line instead. **Lay one straight line through the middle of the readings, about as many above as below,[^1] with short sticks spread along it, take its gradient from two points on the line far apart, and pin it through zero only when the physics says so.**

analogy.text: A needle that wavers on an analogue meter, say on a load that keeps changing a little, is read at the middle of its swing, not at the top or the bottom. A fitted line does the same for readings: it sits in the middle of their scatter, with about as many above as below, and that middle is what you trust rather than any one reading.
analogy.breaks: A needle gives one number, so finding the middle of its swing is the whole job. A line has to get two numbers right at once, its height and its slope, so it can split the readings evenly and still be tilted, as the pinned line does. And a needle's swing is spread over time at one setting, while readings are spread along x, each at a different temperature or load.

practice.text:
- Plot the readings on scales that use most of the graph.
- Lay one straight line through their middle with a ruler, about as many readings above as below. It need not touch any of them.
- Check the sticks: short, with the readings above and below spread along the line, not all above at one end and all below at the other.
- Fit the straight part only. Leave out readings where the graph has clearly bent away.
- Pin the line through (0, 0) only if the physics says y is 0 when x is 0.
- Mark two points on the line, far apart, and take the gradient from them, in y's unit per x's unit.
- Find c by putting one of those points into y = mx + c.
- Write the law. The MCA's syllabus for second engineers writes it as y = ax + b.[^11]
- Check the law against a reading or two: each should miss by no more than the scatter.

**Rule of thumb:** read the law from the line, never from the readings.

**Worked example:** example winding readings at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C are 6.4, 6.5, 7.0, 7.1, 7.6 and 7.7 Ω. Lay a line through their middle passing 6.3 Ω at 10 °C and 7.8 Ω at 60 °C: three readings sit above and three below, each 0.1 Ω off, spread along it. Gradient = (7.8 − 6.3) Ω ÷ (60 − 10) °C = 1.5 ÷ 50 = 0.03 Ω per °C. c = 6.3 − 0.03 × 10 = 6.0 Ω. So R = 0.03T + 6.0: the winding gains 0.03 Ω for each degree, and the line carried back puts it at 6.0 Ω at 0 °C. Check at 30 °C: 0.03 × 30 + 6.0 = 6.9 Ω, against a reading of 7.0 Ω, 0.1 Ω off, the size of the scatter.

**Common mistakes**
- Joining the dots. The zigzag copies every reading's stray, and its gradient changes at every reading.
- Taking the gradient from two readings. 6.5 Ω at 20 °C and 7.0 Ω at 30 °C give 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05 Ω per °C, not 0.03.
- Forcing the line through zero. 7.7 Ω ÷ 60 °C is about 0.13 Ω per °C, because it leaves out the 6.0 Ω the winding has at 0 °C.
- Trusting the count alone. A line can leave three above and three below and still be tilted, with all the readings above at one end.
- Taking two points on the line close together. A small slip in reading either height becomes a big slip in the gradient.
- Fitting the bent part. A spring's readings past the limit of proportionality give a gradient that is not its spring constant.
- Using the first reading as c. 6.4 Ω is the reading at 10 °C, with its stray, not R at 0 °C.
